newsitem.title: ERITREA: Eritrea-Yemen arbitration to start next year.
newsitem.headline: Eritrea-Yemen arbitration to start next year.

text.p: Eritrea's foreign minister said on Wednesday a five-member arbitration panel would convene by next April to decide a territorial dispute with Yemen over Red Sea islands.
Foreign Minister Petros Soloman told Reuters in an interview an agreement to be signed on Thursday in Paris creating an arbitration court would set a deadline of the end of this year for nominations.

"There are two agreements. The one we signed in May was the agreement of principles, which said we would go to arbitration, refrain from using force, and to abide by the verdict of the arbitration tribunal," he said.
"This agreement which will be signed in Paris tomorrow (on Thursday) is an arbitration agreement. It holds the terms of reference for the tribunal and procedural matters.
"Names of the nominees (for the arbitration tribunal) shall be provided before December 31. After that, they shall meet immediately to chose the president," the foreign minister added.
The tribunal, which he said would have five members, will decide sovereignty over the Hanish islands as well as maritime boundaries in the Red Sea.
Eritrea and Yemen will select two members each and the fifth and presiding member will be selected by those four.

If they fail to agree, a presiding member will be chosen by the International Court of Justice in the first three months of next year and the tribunal would start work within the first three-and-a-half months of 1997, Petros said.
Arab Yemen and African Eritrea, facing each other across the Red Sea, claim sovereignty over the small, arid Hanish islands.

They asked the United Nations to mediate after the dispute triggered clashes which killed at least 12 people last December. U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali turned the process over to France, which offered international arbitration.
The islands are near shipping lanes used by more than 100 ships daily, carrying 125,000 barrels of oil from Gulf producers to Europe via Egypt's Suez Canal.
